extracted.intended_audience: news editors and journalists (editors assessing possible plagiarism)
extracted.subtask_description: A short practical guide for editors to determine whether a news article contains unoriginal work (plagiarism) and what form or severity it may take. Focuses on questions to ask, thresholds to apply, and common categories of unoriginality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Using someone else’s words or original ideas without attribution (Norman Lewis’s definition). This focuses on the act itself and not intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the baseline for whether unoriginality occurred; reserve questions of intent for judging severity or penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is any language or the central idea unoriginal?
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by asking: Is some of the language in the article unoriginal? Is the central idea of the story unoriginal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either answer is yes, proceed through other attribution and copying checks to determine whether it rises to plagiarism or a lesser offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to set off verbatim language with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the author fail to set off unoriginal language or ideas with quotation marks?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation marks are the clearest indicator of attribution; a lack of quotation marks (and no citation) suggests failure to attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to attribute via paraphrase or citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the author fail to attribute the work in some other way, such as providing a paraphrase with credit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrasing without credit can be used to conceal copying. Proper attribution can mitigate charges, but absence of credit supports a finding of unoriginality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven- to ten-word verbatim threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the author lift more than seven consecutive words verbatim from another source? (A 7–10 word threshold is a useful guideline.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kelly McBride and Norman Lewis note that seven consecutive identical words are unlikely to be incidental; this is a guideline, not an absolute rule. Consider context (unique phrasing, technical terms, common expressions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution hierarchy: quotation marks then citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution is the opposite of plagiarism; the clearest indicator is quotation marks, followed by citation or other credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explicit markers of sourcing (quotes, named source, link or byline credit). An obligatory h/t or boilerplate credit may not be sufficient if the text is otherwise presented as original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider intent only for severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between whether plagiarism happened (an act) and whether the author intended to plagiarize; intent is relevant to how serious the offense is, not to whether copying occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining consequences, weigh factors like intent, scope, and harm, but use the act-based definition to establish unoriginality first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-plagiarism (recycling one’s own work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing one’s own previously published material without acknowledgement (self-plagiarism) — debated whether it is true plagiarism or a different violation (ethical vs. ownership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the nuance: some editors call for different labels; others see it as an ethical or rights issue. Treat according to newsroom policy and the nature/extent of recycling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patchwriting (paraphrase that mirrors source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrases that mirror the source’s vocabulary and syntax, changing only a few words — defined as relying too heavily on the vocabulary and syntax of the source material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with credit, patchwriting can be intellectually dishonest; some consider it a lesser charge than verbatim plagiarism if the source is credited, while others call it equally dishonest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive aggregation without added value
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewriting or aggregating another reporter’s article (even with credit) without offering original ideas or transformation constitutes a form of appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregation without original contribution is one of the less severe forms of plagiarism but still problematic; avoid by transforming the material and adding reporting, analysis, or value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea theft (appropriating original story ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying heavily on another journalist’s original story ideas or concepts (for example, matching a story by interviewing the same sources without acknowledging the prior reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idea theft is common but not intellectually honest; editors should watch for failure to acknowledge prior scoops or original reporting and consider whether credit or attribution is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a decision flowchart/checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a stepwise checklist or flowchart (e.g., the Poynter flowchart) to guide determinations about whether unoriginal work constitutes plagiarism and its severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the sequence: check for unoriginal language/idea, check for quotation marks/citation/paraphrase credit, apply verbatim-word threshold, then categorize type (self-plagiarism, patchwriting, aggregation, idea theft) and decide on severity and response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize a spectrum and multiple categories of unoriginality
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism is an imprecise term that stands for a spectrum of offenses with varying degrees of severity; resources (Plagiarism.org, iThenticate) list multiple specific types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the form of unoriginality (one of many listed types) to determine appropriate editorial action rather than applying a one-size-fits-all label.
